Chapter 53: Monday, February 28th, 2011 - Taylor

Taylor was glad for Monday to roll around, because as much as she enjoyed being in Australia, she also was now in a school that she enjoyed, and was forced to find out whether or not Arcadia even had a school day on Friday. Luckily they didn’t - none of the schools did after an Endbringer incident, because no one wanted to make it obvious which schools the Wards went to - but she was still annoyed.

What was worse was the press conference that the Prime Minister set up. It had largely been a simple gathering to answer various questions, but the number of people who tried asking the exact same question in different ways was annoying. And then there had been the inevitable question from a news agency simply trying to make waves and make someone look bad:

“Jennifer Conley from Sky News Australia,” the woman said. “If you have this technology that can kill and Endbringer, then why didn’t you before, and why haven’t you gone after the other two?”

Taylor had looked out at her and said, “As for why I didn’t before, well, I only got my powers - and therefore the ship - at the beginning of January. If you can manage to figure out how to go back in time, give me my powers earlier - without damaging the current time-line - then I’ve no problem taking out Behemoth and Leviathan. Of course, you have the problem that Behemoth, for example, hit New York City a year before I was actually born, so that ends up a little problematic. And since I like the time-line the way it is - as in existing - I don’t really feel like playing around with the time stream to get rid of them earlier.”

She had leaned forward. “Remember, Jennifer, the Federation has done exploration of the effects of time travel, and screwing with it can be a bad thing. We don’t have their version of Starfleet that deals with nothing but time incursions, so me going back to change something could literally destroy the world if I prevent something from happening. I know I don’t want that.”

“As for your second question? Well, Simurgh was in the air, so I could get at her. My sensors state that Leviathan is in the deep oceans, and my tractor beams don’t go that deep and still work, and the Enterprise is built for space, not for being the world’s biggest submarine. But let’s say that I can figure out how to tractor beam him up - I can’t, let me reiterate and stress that - but let’s say that I can pull the world’s strongest hydrokinetic out of the ocean. Look up the term ‘mega-tsunami’, Jennifer, and decide which countries you want scoured as he fights being pulled up. And Behemoth is even worse! He’s sitting in the core right now. The only way I’m pulling him up is is by boring a hole through the Earth to get at him. That releases pressure. So which continent do you want me to create the new Toba or Krakatoa on?”

Taylor sighed. “I don’t like that I have to wait for those two to surface, because people will die when they surface. But the limits on the technology I have are there. I can’t transport either of them from where they are to somewhere better - until they make themselves known.” Taylor had openly turned away from Miss Conley of Sky News to talk to a different reporter. She knew that there was going to be a hatchet piece on her that night on that network. She’d been right, but Sky News had taken a bit of a beating for it.

It was now Monday, and she was back in Arcadia. More than one person had thanked her, and she was trying to be gracious about it, because she knew how important what she had done was, but she had to admit that it was getting a little … annoying? Bothersome? … that she couldn’t seem to go anywhere in the halls without someone stopping her and thanking her. She was glad for lunch, because the staff had openly said as she walked in that they were watching, and that she deserved the right to eat her own lunch.

The others at the table were nodding at her and Chris simply asked what she’d thought of Australia. “It was big, and a lot of it is empty, but other than that one reporter, I found everyone there to be pleasant. Ten out of ten, would visit again,” she finished with a laugh. “Preferably not with something life threatening going on next time. I think the worst I want to see next time is to potential for sunburn as I lay out on the beach in a bikini.”

“Better not be a Vicky designed bikini, then,” Charlie said. “With your figure, she’ll have you needing portable force field generators just to keep people from blotting out the sun.”

Taylor grinned. “Maybe we can do it as a group and have Vicky design suits for the guys as well. This bunch of people visiting a beach? I think the guys would have issues with keeping the girls away if they were wearing Vicky Dallon originals.”

Dean looked at Taylor. “You do know that Vicky and I aren’t an item anymore, right?”

“Yeah, but it clearly didn’t end badly. I guess you both had a talk and decided to see why you fought so much?” He nodded. “And you two are still friends, clearly - none of this side-eye and thinly veiled insults stuff you get when a couple is trying to pretend that they’re okay when they aren’t. So you’re both mature enough to handle it.” She chuckled. “Of, course, this would require, really, that we end up going during our Christmas break to do it properly, since summer is winding down for them now, and spring is about to happen for us.” She snickered and started to hum something, and when Dennis recognized it, he burst out laughing.

“I think the loveliest time of the year is the Spring, I do - don’t you? Of course you do!” he sang out in a rather nice baritone. This got the rest of the table laughing as they recognized Tom Lehrer’s ‘Poisoning Pigeons in the Park’.

“Sorry,” Taylor apologized, giggling. “If I’m not careful, everything can turn into a song cue. Mom, Dad, and I used to go to sci-fi conventions and listen to filk music.” She looked to Vicky and Amy. “I was singing one of those when we flew up to the Enterprise with you. A writer named Roberta Rogow wrote that to the tune of ‘The Highwayman’. A group called Technical Difficulties wrote a song called ‘Star Sisters’ based off that thing.”

“Filk?” Chris asked before anyone else could.

“No one’s entirely sure where it came from, but the standing story that everyone accepts as true was a misprint in a convention flier talking about a room where singing would take place - folk music. Since the ‘I’ key is right next to the ‘O’ key, everyone assumes that it was a mistype. And everyone showed up to see what this ‘new’ type of music was.” She shrugged. “I look at what’s been going on since before I was born and end up thinking of a song called ‘Lullaby For a Weary World’. Written by an author named TJ Burnside-Clapp.” She closed her eyes and started to sing.


I wonder how my world can live
With all the hate she harbors.
(Sleep, my weary world.)
And I'm scared of how long it may last,
And just how soon it all may end,
And I wish the power to stop it all
Could rest within my hands.


I've seen her people dying for
Such bold and bloody causes.
(Sleep, my weary world.)
And the bodies of the innocent
Just wash up on the lengthening shore
While the rising tide of history
Just ebbs and flows again.


Oh, make me a cradle to rock my weary world.
Make me a gentle voice,
To soothe her when she weeps.
Make my arms strong enough
To hold her when she wakes,
And make me a lullaby so sweet and fine
That I can sing my weary world to sleep.


I wish that I could soothe away
Her jagged shards of hatred.
(Sleep, my weary world.)
And, 'though my hands may bleed and burn,
I'll hold my broken world to me
Until her ugly scars are healed,
And peace may reign at last.


Oh, make me a cradle to rock my weary world.
Make me a gentle voice,
To soothe her when she weeps.
Make my arms strong enough
To hold her when she wakes,
And make me a lullaby so sweet and fine
That I can sing my weary world to sleep.


If her fighting will not stop,
Then I'll hold her that much closer
And sing my lullaby above the noise and pain of war.

And if her bleeding I can't staunch,
I'll bleed along beside her.
But I will not let her go,
No, I'll never let her go.


When the stars have all burned out,
I'll sing to her in darkness.
(Sleep, my weary world.)
And I pray a tender God may find me,
Huddled in the dark and cold,
And grant the weary world I shelter
One more chance to live.


May God grant my precious world
Another chance to live.


She opened her eyes and blushed as everyone at the table was staring at her, and even Dennis was openly wiping away a tear. “Sorry,” she said, suddenly self-conscious.

“For what?” Dennis asked. “For showing us that not only do you have an amazing voice, but that you … I don’t know how to say it, but if there’s anyone on Earth that I would want to have a ship like the Enterprise under their command, I’m realizing that it’s you.” He shook his head. “I know I’m a jack-ass and will continue to be one. It’s part of who I am. But damn, girl! I -“

“I usually end up singing to myself, either because I’m feeling good, or when I need a reminder. Right now it’s a reminder of just how busy I’m about to get for the foreseeable future. Finally getting the companies off the ground, exploring some of the data we’re going to get from the Simurgh’s body, actually starting to set up some sort of training area for people to learn how to be in a Starfleet-like organization. Because someday I’m leaving orbit to do some exploring. Be nice to visit 40 Eridani or Epsilon Eridani over spring break, for example. I think one of those is where the planet Vulcan was supposed to be. But a song like that reminds me that … I guess the best way that I can describe it is that all the work I’m putting in over the next few months and years is trying to sing that lullaby for Earth. Maybe stop her fighting and bleeding.” She reached up and wiped away her own tears. “I need to at least try, you know?”

Dennis nodded. “I just wish my Dad was going to live long enough to see it,” he said softly. “We’ve talked about the changes already. And there’s problems at Medhall right now, so things with him are … shaky. Not that it really matters,” he finished.

Amy looked at him and sighed an exasperated sigh. “I’d berate you for not saying anything to me about it, but your answer is my standard one, I’ll bet, and I can’t argue with it anyway - I don’t take requests, if only because I need a life of my own.” He nodded at her. She looked to Taylor, who nodded and pulled out her communicator.

“Enterprise? I’ll need you to send Bones down when I ask later, okay? Full med kit.” She looked to Dennis. “Cancer, if he’s at Medhall, right? Which type?” He told her, and she said to Enterprise, “You heard that, right? Full kit, aimed at lung cancer. He’ll be working with Panacea.”

“Elixir,” Amy said. “The hearing for emancipation happens Friday, and I suspect I won’t really be welcome in New Wave after that, so since they own the name, I’m using a different one.” She snorted. “New name, same great taste.” Amy blushed immediately at the eyebrow waggle Taylor gave her, and very lightly slapped her arm. “Pervert, not what I meant.” But the laughter around the table made it clear that she knew what Taylor had just done, since the mood had started to get a little heavy at the information from Dennis.

“I guess you never really mentioned it because of Amy’s rule?” Taylor asked.

“That and the fact that he’d had it for years, and it’s only gotten worse. I might have Triggered in despair over not being able to do a damned thing about it, but I got used to it.” He frowned. “It’s amazing what you can get used to.”

Taylor smiled a wry smile. “Like the fact that since between Bones and Elixir here, Medhall is likely to be losing a few patients from their terminal ward. I’m going to have Congress try to demand I help everyone with my medical tech, while also having big pharm trying to prevent any cures from getting released. Because there’s a lot more money in palliatives than there are in cures. Cure is a one-and-done, palliative is recurring.” She shook her head. “Medical is one place that I want to go all out and just say ‘screw it!’ regarding the tech levels, but even there I have the same worries I’ve got with things like replicators and power generation technologies. If you can use it for creation, the you can use it for destruction. And if I released some of that tech, they’d be calling me an Endbringer, because some of the things that tech can do could wipe an amazing amount of the Eastern seaboard off the planet. We need to get far enough along to be able to responsibly handle that stuff. But gods, I wish I could just start opening clinics and get people to come in and get a pill to regenerate their kidneys and stuff like that. But I need to get that cleared with the governments to begin doing that, and we need to get to the point where the materials exist here on Earth to be able to create such medicines. Which means, just like with the technology of power and electronics, we need the tools to make the tools. They’re just medical in this case.”

She paused. “Gods, I talk too much,” she finished with a laugh.

Chapter 54: Monday, February 28th, 2011 - Amy

Chapter Notes

Sorry for disappearing for about a month. Things just got out of hand and I had too much on my plate, and lost track of posting. I'll post this one and another, and probably catch up with the next two tomorrow.

They met outside the school - Amy, Taylor, and Dennis - and Taylor called to her ship. “Three to beam up.” Amy marveled, as she always did, at the process of basically teleporting from Earth to orbit in a matter of seconds. Once up there, Taylor looked at Dennis and said, “I intend to work out a way to get all the Wards up here, whether one at a time or as a group. And it would be nice to officially know somehow that Vista and Missy Biron are the same person, although I couldn’t possibly tell you how that bit of information slipped to me.”

Dennis chuckled, as did Amy. “Well, your sensors clearly told you that, right?” he said. “Couldn’t possibly be that she ‘accidentally’ told a friend her hero identity, because that would be silly!”

Enterprise walked into the room with Sherrel, and Dennis tried very hard to hide that he was having to adjust his pants at the sight of her. She’d clearly been warned to wear at least a holographic uniform, but it was fairly form-fitting, and there was no one who had seen her after Amy had done her work on her that said that the form was anything but delightful to look at. Sherrel’s only comment was “Thank you for the compliment.” She’d looked at Taylor then and said, “I’ve been playing with the holographics on that thing, since it’s a module I can play with on my vehicles, and I think I’ve given it some oomph.”

“I’ll say,” Enterprise said. “I can generate holographic nerves with one of these now!” she said, holding up an emitter anyone who had ever watched Voyager during its run would recognize. She tapped a few things on the console in the transporter room and the Bones hologram appeared.

“So we got a patient to heal up?” he asked in that southern drawl of his. “I assume we’re beaming down to the planet for this?”

“Yes,” Taylor said with a smile.

“I’m just glad I know I’m a hologram, or else I’d prob’ly complain about transporter use, just like my original did. Still amused that someone sweet-talked him into allowin’ his engrams to be used for me.” He got an amused look on his face and said, “Prob’ly used some pretty girl like one ‘a you three to manage it. He always was a sucker for a pretty face, but nothin’ like ol’’ Jim Kirk was!” All for of the ladies in the room, including the Enterprise hologram, blushed at his compliment.

“Shall we head down and heal up Dennis’s father? I think I’d prefer to do it with tech as much as possible, as close to what I think of as modern technology, because we can use that to get a foothold into the medical fields.” She smiled. “I’m going to have fingers in as many pies as I can manage. If the Federation ever manages to follow Enterprise here, they’ll probably consider me to be violating the Prime Directive, but I honestly don’t care. I’m trying to keep the world from self-destructing, and avoid as much ultra-high tech as possible.”

“Don’t borrow trouble, Captain,” Bones said. “Things’ll happen as they happen. And I’ve got access to the same databases Enterprise here does, so I think you’re already doin’ a pretty good job. And you’ve only been at it for a couple months. Imagine in a year or two.”

Amy nodded. “He’s right. In just the last two weeks you’ve changed Brockton Bay immeasurably. About the only two Empire capes anymore are Kaiser and Othalla, and she’s not exactly a combat monster. Now, let’s get ourselves down to Medhall and heal up some people. Now that Bian has managed to get me covered under Medicare rules and I carry this wonderful medical PADD, we’re set!” She looked to Bones. “You’ve got lead if you prefer. I’ll do the healing that we can’t quite see to using Federation tech to cover, since I can heal this stuff, but I agree with the captain here - do as much with tech as we can.”

Dennis led them in and to his father’s bed. “Dad? I’ve been informed by one of my friends that I was something of an idiot,” he said with a small laugh. “If you’re agreeable, we’ve got a couple people here who would like to see what they can do for you.”

The man looked at was a little startled. “I may be a little closer to death than I thought,” he said through a small coughing fit. “DeForest Kelley?”

“Nah, I’m an Emergency Medical Hologram from the starship Enterprise. We thought we’d come and see what we could do for you and some of the others here. We’re going to see what I can do for you first, since her ability to heal can take so much out of her.” He pulled out a tricorder and scanned the man, and then smiled. “Do I have permission to give you what would be considered an experimental treatment in this place and time? In my time, this is considered a standard treatment and will clear up your problem before the week is out.”

“I’m in here,” the man told him. “Every treatment here is considered experimental, so I don’t see a new one being a problem.” Bones pulled out a hypospray and typed a couple times on the tricorder. The medical bag he carried hummed for a moment, and he pulled out a small vial that he attached to the hypospray, then placed against the man’s neck. A momentary hiss later and he stood back up. “That was synthesized specifically for your treatment. No worries about too much or too little medicine. It was tailored specifically for you. You’ll probably end up going to sleep in a little while from it, just because it’s got a soporific in it, but you’ll wake up tomorrow feeling better. By Friday you should register as free of your conditions.”

“Conditions?” Dennis asked before his mother could.

“Yes, there are some side effects from some of his medical treatments here. Standard issues and easily dealt with.” He scanned the man again. “I can already see things clearing up.” He smiled. “You might be able to check out of here by Wednesday. If you don’t mind, I’d like to check up on you again by Friday.”

“I’m agreeable,” Dennis’s father said. “Might be a placebo effect, but I’m already feeling a bit better.”

“Well, it does start working pretty much immediately, so I’m not surprised. It’s also why I warned you about the likelihood of sleeping soon, because your body is going to want to get to work on all that it needs to do to get you healthy.”

“Thank you so very much, Doctor,” Dennis’s mother said, walking over and hugging the hologram after he’d put everything away.

“It was my pleasure, ma’am,” he said, that good-natured Georgia drawl coming through. He tipped a non-existent hat, which drew a laugh out of the people, and Amy led the other two from the hospital room.

In the hallway, they were met by an administrator. “We were surprised by the visit. Can we help with something?”

“Well, we came because my friend from school admitted that his father was undergoing treatment here. I’m learning proper medical treatments from Enterprise’s medical databases, and decided to tag along while he -” at this she motioned to Bones “- worked his magic on the man’s cancer.”

Taylor spoke up. “I would be more than willing to work with Medhall’s medical staff to see about trying to get some of the Federation’s treatments verified for usage amongst the general populace. I think that both my company and Medhall could end up with an agreeable set of terms to allow this.” She pulled out a business card. “If Medhall would be interested, have them call my company’s lawyers so that we can start the conversation properly.”

Bones spoke up. “Would you mind if we looked at some of your other patients? Mainly the ones closest to death? Because we might be able to at least ameliorate some of their symptoms until an agreement can be reached. I might not be the original Leonard McCoy, but I’ve got his desire to help who I can.”

Amy spoke up. “And while it takes a lot out of me, if we run across people who won’t make it another day or two, I should be able to pull them back from the brink enough to come back another day so that they can be worked on more. Of course, with the standard statement that I won’t do it to someone who refuses parahuman healing.”

“Let me call a couple doctors,” the administrator said excitedly. “I can get them to follow you around to make it proper from our paperwork point of view, and I can get this business card to the people who would need to talk to your people,” he finished, looking at Taylor.

It took about three hours for them to finish what they could, and Amy had been happy that none of them had refused parahuman assistance in healing. She’d apologized for not healing them all the way, but it was both draining for her, and she hadn’t properly prepared, because some people were going to need more work. To a person, each one had said that it was all right and that they appreciated what she had done for them. Several families had been crying happy tears that their loved one would be around longer.

When they left the building, there were a handful of reporters outside the building, just at the point of being on public land. “Panacea, what made you decide to come here today?” a reporter from the Brockton Bay Gazette asked.

She took a breath and responded, “A friend of mine from school happened to mention that his father was a patient here. I so often work with Brockton Bay General because they have the nearest thing to a trauma center this side of Boston, so it seems that the ones most in need of instant healing end up there, and I’m there to make sure that those who wish for healing can get it. To my shame, I didn’t remember places like Medhall here, or Our Lady of Mercy downtown. I will be talking with both here and Mercy to see about setting up some times to visit. It’s hard for me sometimes - and my sister Vicky can testify to this - because healing people is energy intensive, and is literally tiring to me. I used to work myself to exhaustion trying to heal everyone.”

“Grey Ghost? May we ask why you’re here as well? And your companion, who I’d swear is Doctor McCoy from Star Trek?”

She laughed. “I’m here because the friend she mentioned is my friend as well, and since Bones here is an Emergency Medical Hologram - if you ever watched Voyager then you know what I mean by that - he’s part of my crew, so I should be here as well.”

“Not to mention the fact that I’m working on getting proper medical training,” Amy replied. “I can only heal one person at a time, and while I know what needs to be done, I don’t yet have the language; the terminology to explain it to another person who isn’t me. I know what I mean, but by learning how non-parahuman medical professionals refer to things, then I can let them know, and maybe we’ll end up with a break-through because I explain something in a manner that they can follow medically, thereby helping them understand what needs to be done to make a medicine that can do what I do.”

She sighed this time. “I said it on PHO a while back, but it bears repeating. I can only heal one person at a time. I want to help the medical technology get to the point where I’m not needed for coming to a place like this regularly; where someone with ovarian cancer can take a series of pills or series of injections and know that they won’t be leaving their family behind. I want to put myself out of business.” She gave a wry laugh. “I can’t, because emergencies always happen. Car accidents, falls, any number of things happen that we have no control over where people are injured badly. Medicines aren’t going to help that, and I’ll be there to at least keep those people alive long enough for other treatments. But if I can work on getting doctors to a point where they can use medicines to do what I do, it frees me to work on other things to help humanity. Unfortunately, I get side-eye from people because I can affect the body directly, and it makes people think of idiots like Nilbog, or that guy Blasto in Boston. Could I do those things? I don’t know. I’ve never had any urge to even think about trying, because I’m all about making people survive. Maybe if I’m not healing all the time, I might be able to learn safe ways of extending life spans. Maybe make people in dangerous jobs a little tougher.” She looked to Taylor. “I can imagine that some of the dock workers wouldn’t exactly complain if I figured out how to give them a Brute 0 or 1 rating, so that they can withstand some of the accidents that can happen on a work site.”

She looked back to the press. “But I’m not talking about trying to make minions or something. I want to help people. If I gave someone a Brute rating, it would be because they were in a job where it was a safety issue, such as in construction or even police and fire work. A little tougher to handle that fire, or maybe withstand some small arms fire, rather than be potentially killed when someone pulls out a .22 long-range.” She shook her head. “I have learned more about the damage that guns can do than I ever wanted to learn, doing the healing I do. And I know that some people are going to be scared by me saying what I’ve said, and I can never completely put them at ease. But think of it this way - if I was going to do something, wouldn’t I have already? I never force healing on anyone - there is always permission asked, because I understand that there are so many reasons why people don’t want to trust parahuman healing. It’s why I want to learn to be a real doctor,” she said. “Because then maybe I can walk up to those same people who say no to my powers, but will say yes to me giving them a verified medical treatment, and I can still heal them. For me, that’s paramount. I’m here to heal and prevent injury where I can.” She reached up and wiped her eyes, just then realizing that she’d felt so much emotion at the concept that she’d leaked a few tears.

Taylor spoke up. “We’re going to likely be entering conversations with Medhall, since some of the medical treatments we want to get released to the public will need to be vetted by the government, and they are already set up to deal with those same regulations. It won’t be immediate, as much as we’d all like it to be, but with luck, it will happen.” She looked down at her wrist and frowned. “Now, unfortunately, the three of us have another appointment we need to get to, so I’m afraid we have to leave you now.” She tapped the comm badge of her uniform and the three of them beamed up to the ship.

“We don’t have any appointment!” Amy said with a laugh after they’d made it to the ship. “You just wanted out of there quickly!”

“Guilty as charged,” she said. Enterprise informed her that she was actually doing exceptionally well, and if she was willing to do so once the PRT and DA had finished hashing things out, they’d sign her up to go for a GED, and then see if she might be interested in some precision vocational training. Sherrel looked over at Taylor, and Amy could see that the woman was shocked that Taylor clearly meant it. She may have been on her front getting suntan lotion applied, but the older girl somehow straightened as she settled back onto the towel. It was clear that Taylor’s simple declaration had done something positive for the motive Tinker.

“Oh, Deena?” Enterprise asked the girl looking at the PADD, having just finished making notes on the last of her homework. “I’ve been disassembling Simurgh’s programming, and there’s some stuff I want you to look at. If you understand it the way I think you will, I want to help you write the paper for publication.”

“Okay,” Deena said, and tapped open the files that Enterprise had sent her. Within five minutes, she had sat up and was leaned over her PADD, clearly reading fast. She was also breathing fast, and her eyes were very wide. “Holy shit,” the girl breathed. “This connects to that conversation we were having about dimensional folding. Holy shit. Not only can we finally make that armor we were talking about that can fit into a wristwatch or whatever you want to wear - necklace, watch, hell, you could probably build it into a dildo if you wanted to wear one all day - and activate it to be covered in an armor that might well withstand a nuclear explosion at ground zero!”

“That was my thought as well,” Enterprise said. “I can’t write the paper and patent the process, but everyone here who understands it can. Putting the necessary power inside the device dimensionally folded permanently would allow an amazing armor. And given some of the tests I’ve done on that rather delightful material Sherrel built for her own personal motorcycle, that would make an excellent lining whether the fun option was on or off. I’d recommend it be standard to be off,” she said with a laugh.

“Yeah,” Sherrel said. “Might feel good, but if you’re running into battle while your armor is fucking you silly, you might not do that well in battle. But why is it a good material for linings?”

“I put it to some tests when I noticed something interesting about it. It absorbs energy from impacts. It can absorb a lot of energy. If a way isn’t found to release it, it will explode, I discovered, but that takes some significant time to build that high, or an impact that is going to hit so hard that the shock wave is going to kill anyone not in some serious armor for a radius of about a half-mile. My tests show that it can negate G-forces up to 500 g. Admittedly it’s possible for someone to withstand an all-over shock at a very high level, but you tend not to walk away from those. The highest level a human has withstood - and I specifically state human due to various parahuman abilities - was 214 g. This material will negate it up to 500, and any over counts from there as if starting at zero. If we can build the armor and feed the energy stored into the dimensionally folded batteries?”

Amy was amused to see Sherrel unfocus, and then start to shudder and shake against the towel in a familiar manner, especially with the way her hips were moving. “Bitch,” she said to Enterprise lovingly. “Get me worked up with your massage, and then hit me with a design issue? We can slip engines into the dimensional space as well, I think. Possibly enough to move a human at starship speeds, but you’d want a ship, if only because it’d get lonely stuck in a suit alone for days on end. But for bouncing around the solar system?”

“About that,” Enterprise said. “I’m learning more, and I’ve nearly found what I’m looking for. There’s an artificial boundary set regarding parahumans and traveling away from Earth. Until I find the signal I need to block, any parahuman who gets more than 500,000 miles away from Earth will die as their parahuman power forcefully disconnects. The ones who set up how powers get granted don’t want people leaving the nest, apparently.”

Chapter 58: Wednesday, March 2nd, 2011 - Amy

The school day would have been average, but for Taylor’s actions. She was either dealing with a heightened libido, or - more likely to Amy - a desire to keep her from worrying about the meeting she was heading to. Taylor had quietly informed her that she had decided to join Deena and Charlie in their clothing preference of ‘hologram’, and had given Amy a chance to verify that in a quiet corner of the library. Both girls had exited that verification process with smiles on their faces, and Amy had made sure that Taylor was a little distracted at lunch by resting her hand rather far up Taylor’s thigh. She would neither confirm nor deny whether she had gently rubbed her fingers on the skin she was able to reach … she’d found it odd that Taylor’s worry over her had successfully kept her mind on Taylor and off the meeting that was about to happen.0

She waited outside the conference room that they’d rented for the occasion, with Bian agreeing to sit with her as her lawyer. “I’m here to try to shut down some of the worst offenses. Don’t be surprised if they try to go from family to the business of New Wave in a jump - whichever might be more advantageous to them. They may try to complain about me being here, but remember that by bringing your Aunt Sarah into this, they’ve turned it into New Wave business. If they hadn’t brought her in, then there’d be no need for me being here.”

It was at that point that Sarah Pelham and Carol Dallon showed up. Eyebrows were raised at Bian’s being there, but nothing was said until they were in the conference room together. “May I ask why you have a lawyer present?” Carol asked.

Bian spoke up. “May I ask why New Wave is involved? This was supposed to be a meeting between you and Amy regarding her emancipation, and yet Sarah Pelham was made part of the meeting.”

Sarah spoke up. “It is my understanding that some of the information could have a deleterious effect on the future of New Wave, so it was felt that I should be here.”

“Which neatly explains my presence. Since business is involved and you have New Wave’s lawyer here, I felt that it was best if Amy had a lawyer present as well.” When Carol started to open her mouth, Bian continued. “You can’t have it both ways. If business is being involved, then she needs a lawyer present who has some experience with that. Even if you recuse yourself from this meeting as a lawyer and deal only with the maternal aspect of the case, you still have the issue that business is going to be discussed. Therefore she needs a lawyer present.”

The two women paused and walked to the far part of the room to talk in low voices for a bit, but came back over and nodded. “You have a valid point,” Carol said. “So, shall we get started?”

“Yes,” Amy said, choosing to take control for the moment. “This is a simple request that is going before the courts. I wish to be emancipated from the Dallon family, since I have both a place to live and an income coming in.” She paused. “That’s sort of redundant, isn’t it? Sort of defined in the word?” She was mildly pleased to see Sarah snicker softly at that, but Carol frowned deeper. “As for why? There are many people who could testify as to how Carol Dallon treats me on a regular basis. It is obvious that Victoria Dallon is treated with far greater respect than I am. She is excessively critical of anything that I do, finding the smallest of flaws to complain about regarding my actions, while merely rolling her eyes at some of the things that earned Victoria that insulting nickname she has regarding damage. I have never felt love from her during my entire time living in the Dallon household.”

“This is quite a step though,” Sarah said. “Leaving the family over this? What about Vicky?”

“Vicky supports me in this. When she commented on some of the ways that Carol treats me, you know it is a problem, because she admits that she can be self-centered.”

“You threatened blackmail!” Carol yelled.

“Point of order,” Bian said before she could build a head of steam. “What she has pointed out - as verified by one of the witnesses of the exchange - was that there was information regarding her adoption that did not look good. That it was, by all accounts, actually illegal. She did not threaten to out you to the public or anything, according to witnesses, one of which is a recording - and before you complain, Maine is a single person consent state - and at no point did she say that she was going to release this to the press. The worst that she stated was to get angry just before she left and yell that she was going to let the chips fall where they may. At no point did she ever say ‘Do this or I go public’, which is the definition of trying to blackmail someone.”

“Do you know how much this could hurt New Wave’s image?” Sarah asked.

“Which is worse?” Amy asked. “Doing something illegal and hoping to hide it forever - or at least until the statute of limitations runs out - or having it come out that New Wave tried to improve the life of a child whom their actions unfortunately deprived of a father? Admittedly by less than legal means, since Marquis was a known nemesis of the Brigade and an adoption would have been denied for the exact reasons that I’m requesting emancipation.”

“How do you mean?” Sarah asked.

“Note that what I say now is speculation on my part, but I believe that it holds up fairly well.”

“Or at least in court,” Bian said. “Not a threat, but necessary for you to think this all the way through.”

“I have no idea why Brandish utterly loathes the very concept of Marquis, but her utter hatred of him is well known in the community, and still occasionally talked about. What is also talked about is her black and white view of the world. Good and evil, law and crime. And if you come from a criminal family, you’re already in trouble, because it’s just a matter of time.”

Carol opened her mouth, but Sarah interrupted. “Don’t. I’ve heard you say things that can easily be taken that way. And some of them you’ve said with witnesses around.”

“So look at me. The daughter of a villain that she hates, and because Aunt Sarah couldn’t afford to raise me alongside her children - and I do not blame you for that,” she said, turning to Sarah, “it was something you had to think of - Carol Dallon has to raise me, because the group as a whole felt guilty.” She sighed. “It also doesn’t help that I have an almost eidetic memory of that specific day. I remember that you were a little surprised that you were able to take him down so easily. That’s because when these ‘big meanies’ attacked the house, he went unconscious because I Triggered. He woke up in time to defend himself, but the fight was easier for you because he didn’t have time to prepare. And I remember the voice of the woman who was threatening to blast a wrecking ball into the closet to get at whatever he was hiding. Which was me. And I can remember the look on the face of that woman the whole time.”

“I thought you Triggered in the store when Vicky got hurt,” Sarah said.

“No, that’s just when I admitted to it, since I wasn’t about to let her die. But I’d been doing little things since I was six. I just knew never to let Carol see that I was, because she’d have freaked out and screamed that I was the second coming of Marquis. That’s what my prepubescent brain was thinking, at least. And as I got older, I never had any reason to get rid of that feeling. I owe the world my healing for free because I can do it. By that logic, she owes it to the world to do her lawyering for free, because she can do it and not many others can. And I am aware of just how ridiculous that claim is. But so is demanding that I be poverty stricken because I happen to have a power that lets me save people’s lives. Note that I don’t demand huge amounts of cash. I’m getting the Medicare payment, basically, for what I do. But I’m doing that at all the hospitals now, including Medhall, and I’m getting money coming in. I see no issue for there being a problem. Yes, it looks good for New Wave that I give away my healing, but people are coming to demand it because it’s free. If I healed up everyone who demanded I fix their stubbed toes or amblyopia, I’d need to work eight hundred hours a week. And there’s only one hundred and sixty eight of them in that aforementioned week. And that wouldn’t allow for any sleep.”

She leaned forward. “Vicky means so much to me. She’s always been there for me. And Dad? He’s amazing as well. He tries so hard through his depression, and it seems like my adjusting his hormone levels has helped.”

“I thought you couldn’t do brains?” Carol snarked.

“I have never tried,” Amy said in a tired tone. “Too great a possibility to change the core person. But that wasn’t touching his brain at all. It was changing the levels of the chemicals that the body makes elsewhere and sends to the brain. Seratonin, dopamine, that sort of thing. No touching the brain at all. But by making sure his body was putting them out at the same levels I tend to see in other people - adjusted for body weight and such, of course - it seems to have had a positive effect on his depression.”

She looked at Carol. “But in front of both your sister and my lawyer, you showed your attitudes. You didn’t thank me for helping him, you automatically assumed that I had done something wrong, and that I was lying to you all this time about not touching brains.” She pinched her nose. “Has it never occurred to you that if I was that capable and as evil as you hint, New Wave would love me unequivocally? That you personally would never have been able to hate me, because I’d have bio-engineered it out of you? Instead, I sit back and listen to you bitch about how I don’t do enough at the hospitals anymore, and you bitch about my girlfriend - and she’s that in both meanings; friend that’s a girl, and girlfriend - because of the ‘blood will tell’ argument, because her father has grandparents who were Mafia and her mother left Lustrum before she went whackaloon. Lustrum going whackaloon, not Annette, although Danny insists that marrying him proves she was crazy,” she said with a laugh. “But the fact that Danny’s father left the family business behind? Unimportant. Annette followed Lustrum so that meant she followed her always. People change, Carol. All I want is to not live under your roof anymore.”

She opened her bag and pulled out the folder she had with her. “I have no intention of walking into any courtroom with these and saying ‘Your Honor, look at this proof of illegality!’ These are copies of the evidence that my adoption was at the very best hinky.”

“To use a legal term,” Bian said with a snicker, and got one in return from Sarah.

“But these are here to show that I have a legal grounding behind my desire to leave. Agree in court and this never needs come out. Let someone else figure it out; I have zero intention of ‘accidentally’ letting it out, because it would damage New Wave as a whole, and I believe that New Wave does good work out there.” She blushed. “Plus, it would make Crystal and Eric not like me anymore, and even if they aren’t my blood cousins, I want their approval.”

Sarah sat back. “I can’t say that I’m happy about any of this. Especially since I probably should have stepped in a long time ago and seen what I could have done to at least mitigate this issue. We’ve done better monetarily over the years, so Neal and I could have taken you in at some point. And I willfully ignored some of the more egregious things Carol said, thinking that she was just in a mood, instead of that mood apparently being ‘being Carol’.” She spun to her sister and said, “Don’t argue with me on that, we grew up together. I know why you’re the way you are, which is part of why I ignored so much. Allowing the emancipation can be pushed publicly as allowing Amy to spread her wings, whereas if that comes into the public view, New Wave as a whole is tarnished. And you’ve all bitched about how New Wave is my life, and how Laserdream is becoming the new ‘Photon Mom’ because she works so hard for us. So yeah, some of this is me saying that New Wave will look better if you just say, ‘Okay’ in court on Friday, but it also hurts you and Amy less. You can always tell your firm, if they give you side-eye over it, that you two had started bumping heads the way teenagers do, and since she’s old enough to live on her own, you decided to let her. You just don’t admit that you’d prefer to never having her living in your house ever again when you do.”

That last comment surprised Amy, especially because Carol reeled back in her chair with a look of shock and was clearly thinking about what Sarah had said. She opened her mouth to argue a few times, but the words died in her throat every time. Finally, Carol said, “Oh my fucking God. I’ve turned into Dad.” She turned to Amy. “It’s going to take me a lot to get past my upbringing. Sarah handled it better -”

“Differently,” Sarah interrupted. “I think it’s why I threw so much of myself into New Wave.”

“I still say better, but I’ll allow that. But you know my opinion on therapists, and I think that came from him as well. I’ll see what I can do. Friday won’t be an issue for you. I’ll agree to it.” She sighed deeply. “And I’ll try to be accepting about you and the Heb … about Taylor. I never mentioned some of the run-ins with Lustrum’s girls, and some of the attempts that they made to prove that all women are lesbians at heart. So I’ve got issues with her followers and with lesbians.”

Carol stopped and then met her eyes. “I say it in court all the time, so I’ll say it to you. Words are all well and good, but you need proof. So I’ll try. All I ask is that you not avoid me, to give me that chance.”

Amy was surprised by this change from Carol, but it certainly looked real, and she knew that her Aunt Sarah wasn’t good enough of an actress to properly feign the surprise she was showing at what her sister was doing. “I’d like that, Carol. I really would. And honestly, I’d like it if someday we can get to the point where I can decide that I want to call you ‘Mom’. So as long as I’m still allowed around the house, I’m good. I can’t promise often, because I think you heard that one interview outside Medhall the other day. I want to get actual medical training, because I like the idea of the world developing pills and injections that can deal with so many things that only I can heal right now. Well, those fuckers Blasto and Nilbog could if they weren’t assholes, but they are assholes. But I want to put myself out of business.” She snorted. “Maybe give myself the time to work on interesting body modifications, or be the go-to girl for proper sex change operations.”

“Body modifications?” Carol asked, her voice sounding like she was almost worried to hear the explanation.

“A lot of stuff, from giving someone cute little horns, to letting people … well, there’s this whole subculture in Japan - well, was - where some weird sexual things come in. They have words for them, they’re prevalent enough. The one I know about because of the manga - comics - some ABB guy was reading while waiting for healing is called ‘futanari’, which is where someone who is female is also equipped with functional male genitalia. Often while continuing to have their own female genitals. I could spare the thought for how to do something like that if I put myself out of business healing diseases. And those sort of ‘surgeries’ would not be covered by insurance, so I’d charge for it. The more extreme the change, the higher the cost. Sex change can often be covered by some insurances, so I’d accept insurance rates on that. Or keep the cost low for those without insurance, because you don’t tend to do that massive a change just because you’re wondering today what it’s like to be the opposite sex.” She shrugged. “From talking to some of my friends at school, I suspect that if I was willing to pay them, they’d even allow me to do final testing on some of the simpler modifications, like how to do horns that will grow properly. But that’s way in the future.” She grinned. “Not ‘til Sunday, easy.” She managed to tease a real laugh out of Carol with that, and saw Sarah relax.

Carol nodded. “It’s going to take a while, and I’m sorry for that. But I think it would be nice to learn about the girl I’ve been ignoring all these years. And I hope you’ll forgive me if I backslide.” She sat back and shook her head. Softly, she added, “I do not want to turn into Dad any more than I already have.”

“As long as you admit that you’re backsliding and trying to stop it, I’ll be able to forgive you,” Amy said.

“That’s the best I can ask for. I think I said it, but I won’t fight Friday.” After a pause. “And maybe after you’ve got an apartment somewhere, I can bring you a housewarming gift? I’ll have Sarah vet it to ensure that I’m not sending a message I don’t mean to.”

Amy smiled at that. “I’d like that.” With that, the meeting was clearly over, and they all stood to leave. Both Sarah and Carol hugged Amy on the way out, also shaking Bian’s hand.

When she knew they were completely out of earshot, Amy said, “That was different than what I expected. Not unwelcome, though.”

Chapter 60: Friday, March 4th, 2011 - Taylor

To say that Taylor was annoyed would be underselling it. Now that she was in a school where she had friends, and was being challenged by her classes, she enjoyed being there. But now she was being asked to be out of school on a regular basis for various reasons. Today was going to the trial of Sophia Hess. That one had surprised her, because she was sure that the higher ups in the PRT were going to try to keep her out of the public eye in every way possible. Bian had told her that the point was made that if only Emma went to trial, when it was known that Sophia was the main instigator, it would pretty much out Sophia as a parahuman if they insisted on her not being publicly tried, whereas the PRT could step in if there was a conviction and say that since her actions caused someone to Trigger, they would have a say in her punishment, to ensure that she understood the severity of her crime. It was a thin fiction, but it would work for the Unwritten Rules.

So she was sitting in the ante room waiting for the prosecution to call her in. The prosecutor apologized, but she was going to be dredging up some bad memories regarding her time at Winslow. Eventually, she was called into the courtroom.

It looking as you’d expect a Brockton Bay courtroom to look - worn and tired, much like the people who often sat before the judges. Taylor felt that they certainly did their best to make the place spotless, but there’s only so much a cleaning crew can do for a room that has been in use for decades. It really needed to be closed down for renovation.

She was led to the stand where she swore her oath to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and then she sat down. The prosecutor started. “When was the first time you met Sophia Hess?” she asked.

“The first time I saw her, or the first time I met her and found out her name?” Taylor asked.

“Let’s start with the first time you saw her, since it seems to be different from actually meeting her.” There was an objection from defense, but it was overruled.

“The first time I saw her was when I was twelve, and I had gone over to Emma Barnes house after I had gotten home from summer camp. She’d been my best friend - really, a sister in everything but blood - and I wanted to catch up with her, since she hadn’t been able to go to the same camp with me. I got to the house, she answered, and informed me that I was a weakling and that she didn’t want anything to do with me ever again. A person at the door could look down the hallway toward the living room, and saw this girl that I later learned was Sophia Hess standing there, with a look on her face that I registered as smug.” There was another objection, and the statement was amended to, “I can’t say that she was smug, it’s just that the look seemed that way to me. It could be her resting face, for all I knew at the time.”

“Resting face?” the prosecutor asked.

“When people are just sitting there without intending to register any emotion, some have a face that looks like they’re expressing something. The crude version I’ve heard referred to - and I apologize if the reference is considered swearing - but I’ve heard it called ‘resting bitch face’, where a person looks angry or disapproving, even though they aren’t actually intending to express any emotion. For all I knew at the time, what I saw as ‘smug’ was Miss Hess’s regular expression.”

“When were you introduced to Miss Hess?” the prosecutor asked.

“First day of Winslow, when Miss Barnes walked up with Miss Hess and informed me that she had a better friend now and that she didn’t need me anymore. She introduced her by name at that point, and I still had no reason to believe that the first expression I saw wasn’t her resting face.”

“What happened then?”

“Immediately that day? Nothing, other than blatantly ignoring me. The sort of thing where you make sure the person knows they aren’t paying attention to you by making sure that they know where you are in order to snub you? General teenager stuff.” That drew a laugh from the prosecutor, a small smile from the judge, and a scowl from Sophia.

The prosecutor then led her through reading some of the emails that the trio had sent her over time, focusing almost entirely on Sophia’s attacks, except when a post by Emma or Madison mentioned that something had been Sophia’s idea.

She then walked to the prosecutor’s table and opened a box. “I apologize for this, Miss Hebert, but I am about to show you Exhibit 138. Please tell me if you recognize it.” The prosecutor slipped nitrile gloves on and pulled out a battered and bent flute from the box. Taylor’s breathing stopped for a moment.

“I’d have to look closer for a couple telltale markings, but it looks from here as if it is the flute that was referenced in some of the emails. My mother’s flute that they admitted to destroying.” The prosecutor had her assistant bring nitrile gloves to Taylor, who put them on and then carefully took the flute from the prosecutor. She carefully turned it in various directions and rotated it, and began shaking. “This is the flute,” she said in a shaky voice. “Her name was engraved on it, and the engraver actually did small roses to bracket the ‘Annette Rose’ for free. There’s also an odd blemish on the part that has the mouthpiece that is apparently a flaw from the manufacturer, and that flaw is visible. If this isn’t the flute, then someone spent a lot of money to make one exactly like it and then ruin it.” She carefully handed the flute back to the prosecutor with a look of longing in her eyes. She managed to steal a look at Sophia, who was grinning nastily at the table at seeing Taylor’s reaction. Taylor then looked to the jury. Some of them had noticed Sophia’s expressions and were not impressed, making notes that Taylor assumed referred to the incident.

Once the flute was back in the box, the prosecutor pointed out that Exhibit 138 had a chain of evidence that led back to Sophia Hess’s hiding spot, where she not only kept lethal loads for her crossbow, but also apparently kept trophies. The flute had been one of them. She then moved on and eventually reached the 4th of January. “What happened that morning?”

“Objection!” shouted the defense lawyer. “Too broad a question!”

Before the judge could say anything, the prosecutor said, “Fine. On the 4th of January, when you arrived at school, was there anything out of place?” Defense objected again, and the question was rephrased again. It became very clearly very quickly to the judge that the defense was trying to prevent any testimony about January 4th from being mentioned in trial. “I suspect that from the defense’s complaints, they are not even willing to stipulate that the 4th of January happened.” This led to another objection that the judge allowed, but informed the Defense that they had better have good objections regarding this date, or there were likely to be contempt of court sanctions. Finally, Taylor was allowed to speak.

“After at least eighteen months of the things that Madison, Emma, and Sophia put me through” - objection; overruled - “I knew something was up because they preferred to face me first thing to tease or taunt me. On days when something bigger was planned, I wouldn’t see them until they were ready to spring whatever they were going to do on me.” Objection; overruled. “I saw them when I got to my locker and was wondering about the nasty grins on their faces, but when I opened my locker, I understood it.” Objection; overruled. “I had just enough time to realize that my locker was full of garbage before I was shoved into the locker by someone who said ‘Get in there with the rest of the filth.’” Objection; overruled. “I was suddenly in pain in my arms and back, and it was later that I learned why. Everything went odd on me, and that was when I Triggered, apparently.” Objection; overruled. “I Triggered, sir,” she shot at him. “That is cold hard fact backed by the PRT and their power testing.”

“Did you recognize the voice of the person who told you to get in the locker?” the prosecutor asked.

“I am willing to state that it sounded to me like Sophia Hess.” Objection; overruled.

The judge called the defense and prosecution to the bench. “I’ve been making a tally here, defense. I hope that whoever is paying you is willing to take into account the fines I’m going to drop on you at the end of the day, because I’d much prefer to think that it’s at their urging that you’re doing this.” There was a nod from the defense attorney. “Charge them for it. It’s going to be expensive. And tone it down, because I don’t want to send you to lock-up for the weekend.” The judge turned to Taylor. “I’d ask you to try to forget what you just heard, but I know that’s nearly impossible.”

“I understand, Your Honor. I won’t talk about it until after the trial is completely over, if even then.”

The trial picked back up, and the prosecutor asked, “You say it sounded like her. Do you have any reason to believe it wasn’t her?”

“Not really. The force I was pushed into the locker was more than I could believe that either Clements or Barnes could easily manage, while Hess is a known athlete in the school; a track star. Since there was force enough to break both arms and my clavicle - I believe that’s in the report by Panacea? - and a voice that sounded like Hess, I have no reason to say that it wasn’t her. But since I didn’t actively see her, since I was facing the wrong way, I can’t state with one hundred percent certainly. Just upper nineties.” She smiled slightly at the end of her comment. “Sorry.”

“No worries. There were people filming at the time, would that surprise you?” the prosecutor asked.

“No. What surprises me is that any one of them actually called the police on what happened. This is Winslow. Unless you’re the one actively being attacked, you stay out of it. Whether or not it’s true, Winslow gets thought of as gang training grounds. You don’t talk about what happens in case you annoy the wrong gang and they decide that you need to learn that kneecaps are a privilege.” There were snickers from the jury. “I can only suspect that when the light came out of the locker, someone thought that was a bit too far and called something like 911 or the PRT.” She shrugged. “I can’t say any more about Winslow, because I literally have not set foot on its property since January 4th.”

She was excused after a few more framing questions, and was told that they might call her back later, but they’d give her as much warning as possible. They were done with her for the day, however, so she was allowed to go home. As she left the courthouse, she was pretty much ambushed by reporters shouting questions at her. She was finally able to get a word in edgewise. “I know you want information, but I don’t want to say anything that might cause a problem for the case. I don’t know that anything I say to you would be a problem, but I don’t want to take the risk. Believe me, I understand where you’re coming from, but I don’t want my words out here to come back and hurt the case. If she’s guilty, then she should be convicted. If she’s innocent, she should be released. For me to say anything to you might damage either of those outcomes.” She shrugged. “Sorry.” With that, she slipped past them and headed down the street for something to eat before heading up to the ship.

Chapter 61: Friday, March 4th, 2011 - Taylor

Chapter Notes

Sorry for the delay in posting. The point I'm at in the story has been kicking my ass, having taken me close to three weeks to get maybe 3,000 words down. For the speed I tend to write, that's a LONG time. The scenes I was working on just did not want to gel, so I was slowing down.

That has no effect on the previously written chapters like this one, but spending so much time on focusing on the 'current' chapter (as in the one I'm writing) caused me to forget to post here.

Hoping I won't have the same issue this weekend.

Once on the ship, she did a quick check to see what was going on. Sherrel was the only other one aboard at the moment, and she appeared to be making a lot of notes on things. “Had a good idea, huh?” she asked Enterprise.

“I figured out how to attempt to talk to the source of a person’s powers, and she insisted on being the first, so that if it was a danger, you wouldn’t be at risk. She spent some time conversing - I heard her side of the story mostly, but was able to detect and somewhat decipher the other side as well. They apparently call themselves ‘shards’ as parts of a crystalline whole that are intentionally shed to grant powers. Would you like me to connect you with yours, since there doesn’t seem to be an issue with Sherrel, other than a flurry of non-fugue Tinkering?”

“I would find that an extremely interesting concept,” Taylor replied with some excited amusement.

“You may wish to sit down for this. I also wonder if you will have the reaction that Sherrel did.”

As she sat down, Taylor quipped, “I don’t know if that sounds ominous or not.”

“Let’s go for ‘not’,” was Enterprise’s amused response. “I’m going to be starting now,” she added.

Taylor, being in contact with the ship in a way at all times, could feel what Enterprise was doing via subspace. She could almost make out the communication happening, and suddenly she felt something in her mind. It was vast, yet somehow at the same time smaller than Enterprise felt. But the depth of knowledge she could feel was immense.

[Salutation]

Taylor was stunned at the comment in her mind, and felt Enterprise’s amusement over something. The extra entity also felt amused, and perhaps - in an alien manner - smug.

~Hello. Very information rich communication there. Your name translates out to ‘Queen Administrator’, or ‘Top Administrator’ or something of the like?~

[Affirmative. Data]

~Wow. Basically a living … well, I’d call it a computer system?~

[Affirmative]

~I am going to be asking you so many questions over time as they come to me, the same way that I do the ship you connected me to. And I want to thank you for that as well.~

[Data]

~It may be your purpose, but you connected me to another highly intelligent computer system that is now my friend, so appreciation is due. I am hoping that you and I could potentially end up as friends as well. We are sort of stuck with each other for the rest of my life.~

[… Data]

~Well, it’s how you connect. I’ve heard of situations where someone tried removing the two masses in the brain and died despite all the care taken. As long as you’re not trying to kill me, the way it seems one parahuman - ~

[Query]

~Parahuman is what we call people that your people grant powers to.~

[Query]

~Of course you’re people. You’re intelligent, as opposed to the Simurgh, which was really just an impressive robot.~

[Data]

~Simurgh was what we called a specific … wait, can you read my thoughts? If you can, it might be best to figure out from there what it was.~

Taylor felt the presence that she was thinking of a ‘Queen Administrator’ touch her thoughts and could feel the disdain when she found what Simurgh was.

[Data]

~Wow, not a fan of those things, are you? Yeah, we called them Endbringers because they’re such a pain to fight; they pretty much kill everyone that comes near them. Hence End Bringer. Until you connected me to Enterprise. We carved Simurgh up, and read her programming. It’s how Enterprise figured out how to allow you to connect to me, and a friend’s Shard to connect more directly to her. Hoping we can set up some sort of a secondary network where we can talk via you Shards.

[Smug]

Laughing, Taylor responded, ~That came through with so much emotion in it that I got that before I got the [Data] from you! So networking is what you … of course it is. You can’t be Queen Administrator if you’ve got a network of one. Hence the [Smug].~

[Data]

~I pick things up fast. Doubt I’ll ever completely get down your style of talking, but if I need to send you something data-rich, I’ve an idea how at least. Does Sherrel need to be here, or can you connect to her since she’s nearby?~

[Data]

~Ah, the closer the better. Okay. I can look her up, or wait for the others to arrive, get connected if they want, and then set up our own little network. Is there a distance beyond which the connection won’t work, like the limit on how far away from the planet we can get before we forcibly disconnect?~

[Data]

~Okay, so you can disable that for anyone on the network you’re running, unless The Warrior intentionally overrides, and you have already disabled that for me. How likely is The Warrior to notice?~

[Data]

~We’d call that ‘off in his own world’ here on Earth, but from what I understand, his body is on his own world. He’s pretty much not paying attention to anything?~

[Data]

~Okay, that sounds like mourning. Is his being in charge of things why everyone who gets powers seems to be geared to fight?~

[Agreement]

~Can he be replaced, so that a different drive can be put in place, like creativity? Yes, fighting often makes you think about new ways to use your powers - if you survive long enough. But if you’re driven to think about interesting uses for your powers, well, people can come up with all sorts of interesting ideas that most others wouldn’t think of at first. For example, someone with the power to generate blades might tend to think about how to fight others with them, but if they really aren’t interested in fighting, they might see if they can lace some of them together such as to create a shield. Or they just get lazy and use the power all the time for nothing more than opening packages.~ She smiled at the end of that thought.

[Amusement. Data]

She came back to herself and looked around. Sherrel was in the room, and so were Amy, Vicky, Charlie, and Deena. “We gotta figure out how to get Vista up here on a regular basis. She also wondered if the girl had testified at Sophia’s trial or this one yet, or was going to, because she honestly couldn’t see either trial not wanting one of the major sources on the stand - prosecution to back up everything said, and defense to see how much they could tear down.

Taylor’s testimony was mostly to show that Emma was something of the mastermind of the Trio, and that she orchestrated the attacks most of the time. That had been Taylor’s understanding of the dynamic amongst them, and the direction the questions led seemed to agree.

Emma was not the world’s best actress, in Taylor’s opinion, so the ‘innocent little girl’ look she had on during the questioning didn’t fool Taylor. Of course, she had to admit to herself that she’d stopped falling for Emma’s act a while back and had jut fallen to enduring her crap until the 4th of January, when things had gone seriously out of Taylor’s hands.

The prosecution asked her, “Was Miss Barnes directly involved in the attack?”

Taylor thought for a second. “Physically, I can’t say. But she was saying insulting things to me and I definitely recognized her voice saying that I was in with the rest of the filth, and if I was lucky I’d see my mother again.”

“I’m sorry if this hurts you, but how did you take that?”

“Well, it actually made me pause for a second before the panic and pain set in, because it could have had two meanings, and at that point in our relationship, such as it was, I could take it to have two meanings, either one of them likely. The first one was that my mother was nothing but filth, so I’d be with her in amongst all that crap in the locker. The more likely one, in my opinion, was simply that I’d die in the locker and be with my mother again in the afterlife.”

“Why do you consider that the more likely meaning?”

“Objection, Your Honor,” defense called. “Requires pure speculation.”

The judge thought for a long moment before saying, “Prosecution has been building toward the possibility of motive for a while, and the questioning has shown a knowledge of the defendant. I’ll allow it, but just barely. Do be careful, prosecutor. And you, Miss Hebert.”

“Yes, Your Honor.” She frowned. “I have been the target of Emma’s insults since I returned from summer camp the year I turned twelve. So I like to think that I’ve become knowledgeable about her style when it comes to insults from back when we were six years old. To imply the first one would require a depth of thought that didn’t tend to go into her taunts, because it requires … well, it requires extra thought. I went to Winslow because my friend was going to be there. Emma went there because she couldn’t qualify for Arcadia.”

“Objection!” from defense.

“Proof is already in evidence,” the prosecutor said in an almost bored tone. “I can tell you the evidence numbers if need be.”

“Overruled,” said the judge.

“Sorry, didn’t know that would be a problem,” Taylor said. “But to make the insult about my mother being filth would require a step of logic that wasn’t always in evidence when she insulted people. She was very good at firing off quick insults, but the ones that were the ones that required following a chain of thought tended to be the ones she started off the insults with, since she’d had the time to prepare them, and they tended to come out of her mouth differently; more practiced, I’d say. Her snap insults were always more surface level, easier to come up with on the fly. If she meant the first, she would have started off with it. So it’s more likely she was saying I should just die.”

Emma was now scowling, and the assistant to the defense lawyer had a grip on Emma’s arm and was saying something in a low tone. It struck Taylor that the lady was telling her not to say what was running through her mind, because that would hurt their case.

“Did she often say that to your face? We’ve had you read many of the emails that we traced back to her accounts and saw those sort of things, but would she say it when directly in front of you?”

“Oh yes, all the time. Wondering why I hadn’t just joined my mother years ago, the way I should have; that she’d died just to get away from me; that there was something mentally wrong with me for crying for a week when Mom died; all sorts of things.” She frowned. “To be honest, I don’t think she really thought about her insults too much, because in her insults I was often simultaneously the ugliest thing that could pass itself off as a human being and also the girl you went to for sex; that I’d screw anything, it didn’t have to even be human.” She shrugged. “Not my worry anymore. I learned to just endure, as frustrating as that was. It got to a point where I considered everything she said as a lie. If she mentioned that it was a sunny day outside, I’d look for an umbrella at the very least. That sort of thing. It felt to me that she only spoke to me to make my life difficult.”

“Objection!”

“Sustained. Be careful, Miss Hebert,” the judge said.

“Apologies. Honesty requires that I admit that my last comment was pure opinion, and only how I saw things. I don’t claim that it’s fact.” She found herself wondering about the prosecution on both cases, and the defense, for that matter. It felt like she was allowed to talk a lot more than either lawyer probably should have allowed her to, but she didn’t know anywhere near enough about the law to say, and realized that to some extent, it might have simply been the style of the given lawyer. The last comment just before her apology had earned a sustained objection, but Taylor knew that the jury would still remember hearing it.

They finally released her from the stand and asked her to wait in the anteroom until the day was over, which wasn’t too much of an imposition now that she had access to the new mental network. She felt out to see what was going on with the others, and smiled at the various things. It was now afternoon, so the four girls she went to school with were now aboard the Enterprise, finishing up homework and then trying to learn things to be more useful aboard the ship, while Sherrel was still writing down all the ideas that she had been having over the last few days. Even with Enterprise supplying the materials, Sherrel probably had about a month of building ahead of her if she did nothing but build, sleep, and eat. Chapter 64: Friday, March 11th, 2011 - Taylor

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

The girls were mildly amused at Amy’s reaction to actually wearing the ankh armor. It certainly did display that the girl had larger nipples than most girls, and gave the strong impression that there were nipple rings keeping the crossbar up and covering her breasts. She hadn’t worn it in public yet, but thought she might when the summer came, to look as if it were more of a swimsuit. Taylor was suggesting to her that this was an excellent idea.

Taylor had done as she had said and had a few tunics made with the Minoan breast cutout made, and she wore those around the ship. Those turned out to be popular enough - and more importantly comfortable enough - that the others picked up the habit as well. Amy was officially a member of the Enterprise crew, and wore a uniform pretty much the moment she came on board from the planet. She occasionally had to be reminded that her breasts were visible when she went to return to the planet, because she had forgotten what she was wearing. Vicky was smiling when she realized that, and wiped a fake tear away from her eyes. “My sexy sister is growing up and letting people know she’s hot!” Amy blushed at that, but also laughed.

The group worked in the holodeck on some scenarios, and on Friday felt ready to do at least a beginning patrol. All of them except Taylor chose to wear the helmeted version of the armor, hiding their faces. Taylor decided not to have the armor form fit her too much, until people were a little more used to her, so the armor didn’t show the complete outline of her nipples and areolae yet. She was noticeably pointy, however. Charlie actually chose to let the outline of her heart-shaped areolae and nipple be visible through the armor. They chose a spot on the Boardwalk and beamed down.

Enterprise told them that they were likely to meet up with a Wards patrol partway through their own patrol, so Taylor was pleased, because it meant that they could make it abundantly clear that the two groups were friendly. They started walking down the Boardwalk, and there were definitely people using their phones and video cameras to film them.

Someone finally took the chance to step forward. “Is this an all-female team? I mean, it’s obvious at the moment that there’s nothing but females here, but is it permanently girls only?”

Taylor smiled at the girl who had asked. “No, it’s just the way things have fallen at the moment. Haven’t been around long enough to have grown a huge group yet. I’m in the process of working on what I need in order to set up an academy to train people how to … well, deal with my ship, really. Technology and so many other things. Right now it’s just that I’ve mostly been - well, attracting is probably the wrong word, given connotations, but let’s use it anyway - attracting girls to my group.” She felt a … something … pass through the mental ‘group chat’, and suddenly all of her team were retracting the helmets into the armor.

“Cool effect!” someone else said.

Vicky spoke up. “I’m still a member of New Wave, but I’m also a friend of Captain Hebert’s, so when she mentioned that she wanted to start patrolling, I felt it was a good idea to help out.”

“Does the group have a name?” someone else asked.

“Right now I think of them as my away team,” Taylor said with a laugh, “so ‘Away Team’ sounds as good as anything at the moment.” There was some general laughter.

“What’s the armor made of?” a boy about Taylor’s age asked.

“Not to be a smart-ass about it, but something that wouldn’t make any sense to you if I told you, because the current Earth tech doesn’t have a name for it yet. But it’s very tough and very resilient, and that’s even without the liner that negates an amazing amount of G-forces. It flows onto us sort of like a liquid - think nano-technology, even if that’s not really the explanation, so no worries about a grey goo situation - and settles into a decently form-fitting armor.”

“Well, it looks like it’s got some excellent forms to fit,” came the technology-distorted voice of Dennis.

“Thank you, Clockblocker!” Amy replied, bowing floridly at him. He returned it with as much pomp as she had given.

“Seriously though - and yeah, I know; this is me saying it - I meant it more as an appreciation of -”

“We know what you were appreciating, Clock,” Vicky interrupted with a laugh.

“Guilty as charged, because you’re all beautiful, but I was actually commenting on your level of fitness. It’s good to see people who decide to patrol as heroes taking the time to actually get into a shape where they’re not going to be gasping for breath if they have to run.” Taylor liked that he tossed off a public relations comment to point out that heroing was not just ‘put on costume; fight crime’.

“Well, given some of the stuff that needs to be done aboard the Enterprise, being fit only makes sense. Even with grav units to help lift stuff, it doesn’t negate the mass of what you’re moving, so you need some muscle with some of the stuff you’re going to move, if only to control its movement. You do not want to get a high mass item moving at high speed unless you want it to be a projectile.”

“I’ve got to admit, I’d love to visit your ship,” Clockblocker said. “I’m jealous of Vista here, even if all she really got to see was a couple hallways.”

“And the bridge,” Vista said. “We used the Captain’s Yacht, remember.”

Clockblocker’s body language made people chuckle, because it was clearly screaming ‘humorous pout’. Taylor said, “Get the PRT to give permission, and I have no issue with setting up some point when I can invite all of the Wards who want to visit up to the ship. Even see if the Tinkers in the group have the same reaction that the former villain who was known as Squealer had to Federation technology.”

“Former villain?” one of the adults in the audience asked.

“Yeah. Got her up there to save her life after Skidmark attempted to beat her to death with a crowbar because she couldn’t build something at the speed and design he wanted built - let’s just ignore actual physics and demand it be built when he wants it built - and once we cleared the crap out of her system that Skidmark had addicted her to, she’s been amazing.
